facts.statement: The type species of the genus is Leptoceratops gracilis.

facts.statement: Leptoceratops was first discovered in Alberta in 1910 and named in 1914 by Barnum Brown.

facts.statement: Charles M. Sternberg uncovered three additional skeletons of Leptoceratops in the Scollard Formation in 1947.

facts.statement: Leptoceratops had a very large head with a strong jaw but lacked horns and possessed only a very reduced frill.
facts.quote: The head is very large with a strong jaw, but lacks horns and has a very reduced frill.

facts.statement: Leptoceratops was approximately 2 meters long and possessed a mix of primitive and derived ceratopsian features.

facts.statement: Leptoceratops likely moved bipedally at high speeds and quadrupedally when moving slowly.
facts.quote: Leptoceratops was likely bipedal when moving at speed and quadrupedal when moving slowly.

facts.statement: Leptoceratops had unique teeth among dinosaurs that showed wear patterns driven by a mammal-like jaw rotation during chewing.
facts.quote: The teeth of Leptoceratops are unique among dinosaurs, showing tooth wear in a fashion that must have been driven by mammal-like rotation of the jaw while chewing.

facts.statement: Leptoceratops had an efficient bite capable of processing various food types including angiosperms, conifers, and cycads.
facts.quote: This, along with the handling of stress in the jaws, show that Leptoceratops had an efficient bite allowing it to be adaptable to different food types, such as the angiosperms, conifers, or cycads found in its environment.

facts.statement: Leptoceratops inhabited a semi-humid floodplain environment with braided streams and small-treed forests.
facts.quote: The environment inhabited by Leptoceratops was a semi-humid floodplain region with regular braided streams and small-treed forests.

facts.statement: It is possible that Leptoceratops dug and lived in multi-generational burrows.
facts.quote: It is possible that within these environments, Leptoceratops dug and lived in multi-generational burrows.

facts.statement: Two ceratopsian specimens were discovered in 1910 along the Red Deer River in Alberta by an American Museum of Natural History expedition.
facts.quote: A 1910 expedition by the American Museum of Natural History (AMNH) discovered two ceratopsian specimens from the Maastrichtian age of the Cretaceous along the Red Deer River in Alberta, Canada.

facts.statement: In 2013, nine specimens of Leptoceratops were found in the lower portion of the Scollard Formation, dating to approximately 65.5 to 66.1 million years ago.
facts.quote: Within the Scollard Formation, Leptoceratops was known in 2013 from nine specimens found in the lower portion, with an estimated range of 65.5-66.1 million years old (0.5 my older with recalibration).

facts.statement: Barnum Brown collected an additional specimen of Leptoceratops from the St. Mary River Formation of Montana in 1916.
facts.quote: In 1916, Brown collected an additional specimen, AMNH 5464, from the St. Mary River Formation of Montana.

facts.statement: Charles M. Sternberg established the genus Montanoceratops in 1951 to separate it from Leptoceratops.
facts.quote: Sternberg named Montanoceratops in 1951.

facts.statement: Michael Ramus discovered a Leptoceratops locality in the Lance Formation of Wyoming in 1962.
facts.quote: A Leptoceratops locality was found in 1962 within the Lance Formation of Wyoming by Michael Ramus, where a single individual was collected.

facts.statement: John Ostrom described a Leptoceratops skeleton from Wyoming in 1978, noting its similarity to specimens from Alberta.
facts.quote: Described in 1978 by American palaeontologist John Ostrom, the skeleton is very similar to the material assigned to Leptoceratops from Alberta

facts.statement: Leptoceratops is the namesake genus of the family Leptoceratopsidae.
facts.quote: Together with related taxa, Leptoceratops is the eponymous genus of the family Leptoceratopsidae.

facts.statement: Leptoceratops possessed high-spined tail vertebrae, though not as pronounced as those of Montanoceratops.
facts.quote: The vertebrae of the tail were high-spined, though not as high as those of its relative Montanoceratops

facts.statement: Leptoceratops had robustly built forelimbs and hindlimbs.
facts.quote: The forelimbs and hindlimbs are robustly built

facts.statement: The pectoral and pelvic girdle bones of Leptoceratops were slender and resembled those of earlier ceratopsians.
facts.quote: The pectoral and pelvis girdle bones were slender and more like earlier ceratopsians.

facts.statement: Specimens CMN 8888 and 8887 were found 50 feet above the base of the Upper Edmonton member, with CMN 8889 located an additional 5 feet above them.
facts.quote: CMN 8888 and 8887 were 50 ft above the base of the Upper Edmonton member, and CMN 8889 was an additional 5 ft above them.

facts.statement: Newer geological studies have separated the Edmonton Formation into the Edmonton Group, with Leptoceratops known from the uppermost formation, the Scollard.
facts.quote: Newer geology has separated the Edmonton Formation into four formations as the Edmonton Group, with Leptoceratops known from the uppermost named the Scollard Formation

facts.statement: In 2004, Chinnery questioned the assignment of specimen YPM VPPU 018133 to Leptoceratops due to jugal similarities with Prenoceratops and potential locality issues.
facts.quote: The assignment of YPM VPPU 018133 to Leptoceratops was questioned by Chinnery in 2004, as the jugal is similar to that described for Prenoceratops and the locality may be part of the Meeteetse Formation instead.

facts.statement: Leptoceratops was first discovered in 1992 in the Hell Creek Formation of Montana by Brig Konecke.
facts.quote: Leptoceratops was first found in the Hell Creek Formation of Montana, equivalent in age to the Scollard and Lance Formations of Alberta and Wyoming, in 1992 with the discovery of a rear part of a skull by Brig Konecke.

facts.statement: The holotype skull (UWGM-200) was prepared in 1998 and contains the first complete braincase described for the genus.
facts.quote: The skull, University of Wisconsin-Madison Geology Museum number 200, was prepared in 1998 and shows the first complete braincase yet described.

facts.statement: A dentary bone found in 1995 in Alberta was initially identified as Leptoceratops but is now classified as the separate genus Unescoceratops.
facts.quote: An isolated dentary of a protoceratopsian, TMP 95.12.6, was found in 1995 by Canadian palaeontologist Philip J. Currie in the middle Dinosaur Park Formation of Alberta, which is middle Campanian in age.

facts.statement: Leptoceratops is characterized by a large head, a minimal frill, and a body structure suggesting it was primarily quadrupedal.
facts.quote: Leptoceratops was an unusual early ceratopsian, displaying a very large head but minimal frill, a more forwards center of mass suggesting quadrupedality, and a higher number of vertebrae in front of the pelvis.

facts.statement: A reconstructed complete skeleton of Leptoceratops measures approximately 1.81 meters in length.
facts.quote: The complete skeleton of CMN 8889, with the tail of CMN 8887 added and scaled up to match the other bones, measures 1.81 m in length.

facts.statement: The largest known individuals of Leptoceratops reached about 2 meters in length and weighed 100 kilograms.
facts.quote: The largest individuals of Leptoceratops were likely around 2 m long and weighed 100 kg.

facts.statement: Leptoceratops skulls are lower and longer than Protoceratops and uniquely lack a crest at the back of the skull.
facts.quote: The skull of Leptoceratops is similar to Protoceratops in general form, but is lower and longer and uniquely lacks a crest at the back of the skull to make a prominent frill.

facts.statement: Complete Leptoceratops skulls range from 330 mm to 450 mm in length, with corresponding mandibles measuring 275 mm to 345 mm.
facts.quote: The complete skulls known range from 450 mm long in CMN 8889 to 330 mm long in CMN 8887, with respective mandibles 345 mm and 275 mm long.

facts.statement: Leptoceratops lacks nasal and postorbital horns, distinguishing it from more derived ceratopsians.
facts.quote: There is no horn on the nasal unlike more derived ceratopsians, nor on the postorbital.

facts.statement: A large ridge on the maxilla suggests Leptoceratops had a muscled cheek pouch to help shred large amounts of vegetation.
facts.quote: There is a large ridge above the teeth on the maxilla, which would have supported a large muscled cheek pouch to assist in shredding large amounts of vegetation.

facts.statement: Leptoceratops teeth exhibit a unique type of tooth-on-tooth wear shared only with Udanoceratops and Archaeoceratops.
facts.quote: The teeth in Leptoceratops are some of the most distinct in Ceratopsia, showing a unique type of tooth-on-tooth wear only shared with taxa such as Udanoceratops and Archaeoceratops.

facts.statement: Leptoceratops possesses the largest single-rooted teeth of any ceratopsian, whereas ceratopsids have split, double-rooted teeth.
facts.quote: Leptoceratops teeth are also the largest in absolute size of any ceratopsian with single-rooted teeth; the tooth roots of ceratopsids are split to be double-rooted.

facts.statement: Fossil material of Leptoceratops was found 75 meters below the Cretaceous-Paleogene boundary in the middle Hell Creek Formation.
facts.quote: UWGM-201 was found 75 m below the Cretaceous-Paleogene boundary in the middle Hell Creek.

facts.statement: The related fossil TMP 95.12.6, originally thought to be Leptoceratops, dates to the middle Campanian age.
facts.quote: An isolated dentary of a protoceratopsian, TMP 95.12.6, was found in 1995 by Canadian palaeontologist Philip J. Currie in the middle Dinosaur Park Formation of Alberta, which is middle Campanian in age.

facts.statement: Complete vertebral columns in Leptoceratops specimens CMN 8888 and CMN 8887 measure 1.66 meters and 1.35 meters in length respectively.
facts.quote: Complete vertebral columns of CMN 8888 and 8887 are 1.66 m and 1.35 m long respectively

facts.statement: The number of tail vertebrae in Leptoceratops varies by specimen, ranging from 38 to 49.
facts.quote: The number of caudal vertebrae varies, with 38 in CMN 8887, 48 in CMN 8888, and 48 or 49 in YPM VPPU 18133

facts.statement: Humerus lengths in Leptoceratops specimens range from 185 mm to 290 mm.
facts.quote: The humeri, 290 mm long in AMNH 5205, 242 mm long in CMN 8889, 255 mm long in CMN 8888, and 185 mm long in CMN 8887

facts.statement: Femur lengths in Leptoceratops specimens range from 230 mm to over 270 mm.
facts.quote: The femur, which is 270 mm long in CMN 8889, 265 mm long in CMN 8888, 230 mm long in CMN 8887, and over 257 mm long in YPM VPPU 18133

facts.statement: Leptoceratops had a complete hand with two rows of wrist bones and three toes equipped with hooves.
facts.quote: The hand is complete, displaying two rows of carpals, and three digits with hooves on the first three

facts.statement: The finger bone arrangement in the Leptoceratops hand follows the formula 2-3-4-3-1.
facts.quote: The manus has a phalangeal formula of 2-3-4-3-1

facts.statement: The foot bone arrangement in Leptoceratops follows the formula 2-3-4-5-0.
facts.quote: The pes has a phalangeal formula of 2-3-4-5-0

facts.statement: The first three neck vertebrae in Leptoceratops do not fuse until adulthood, a trait considered more primitive than in Protoceratops and other ceratopsids.
facts.quote: The first three cervicals are not fused together into a syncervical until adulthood, which is distinctly more primitive than Protoceratops and ceratopsids

facts.statement: The shoulder blade of Leptoceratops is slender and similar to Protoceratops but lacks the diagonal ridge found in other ceratopsian genera.
facts.quote: The scapula is more slender than in ceratopsids but similar to Protoceratops while lacking the ridge that extends diagonally across the scapular blade found in the other genera

facts.statement: The arm bones of Leptoceratops show an intermediate build between the slender bones of Protoceratops and the robust bones of ceratopsids.
facts.quote: The humerus, radius, and ulna are intermediate between Protoceratops, where they are more slender, and ceratopsids, where they are more robust

facts.statement: The hip bone of Leptoceratops is primitive, resembling Protoceratops but thinner and lacking the marginal expansion seen in later ceratopsians.
facts.quote: The ilium of Leptoceratops is primitive for a ceratopsian, being similar to Protoceratops but thinner and without any expansion of its margin found in later ceratopsians

facts.statement: The pubic bone in Leptoceratops is proportionally smaller than in Protoceratops, with a posterior process measuring only 50 mm in length.
facts.quote: The pubis is similar but proportionally smaller than in Protoceratops, with a short and narrow anterior process and a curved and tapered posterior process that is only 50 mm in length

facts.statement: The ischium in Leptoceratops resembles that of Protoceratops but lacks expansion at the end or an internal groove near the base.
facts.quote: The ischium is also similar to that of Protoceratops, but does not show any expansion towards its end or internal groove near the base

facts.statement: Leptoceratops had four fully developed clawed toes, with the first slightly outturned, and a fifth toe reduced to a splint-like bone.
facts.quote: The first four digits are fully developed and bear claws, with the first being slightly outturned from the rest, while the fifth digit is reduced to just a splint-like metatarsal

facts.statement: Leptoceratops was originally classified as a primitive ceratopsian outside the family Ceratopsidae.
facts.quote: Leptoceratops was first named as a primitive member of Ceratopsia outside the family Ceratopsidae

facts.statement: Franz Nopcsa classified Leptoceratops within the family Ceratopsidae and created the subfamily Leptoceratopsinae for it.
facts.quote: Hungarian palaeontologist Franz Nopcsa, who instead placed Leptoceratops within Ceratopsidae and in its own subfamily, Leptoceratopsinae

facts.statement: Alfred Romer established the family Leptoceratopsidae in 1927 and placed Leptoceratops within it.
facts.quote: American palaeontologist Alfred Romer, who placed Leptoceratops within the new family Leptoceratopsidae in 1927

facts.statement: Leptoceratops and Montanoceratops were later included within the family Protoceratopsidae based on new material.
facts.quote: The two genera, as well as Montanoceratops after its separation, were included within Protoceratopsidae

facts.statement: Paul C. Sereno suggested in 1986 that the traditional family Protoceratopsidae is paraphyletic.
facts.quote: American palaeontologist Paul C. Sereno suggested in 1986 that Protoceratopsidae as traditionally used is paraphyletic

facts.statement: The name Leptoceratopsidae was adopted for a group of diverse early ceratopsians from the Late Cretaceous.
facts.quote: the name Leptoceratopsidae adopted for the group, which soon included a diverse variety of early ceratopsians from the Late Cretaceous

facts.statement: Recent analyses added Ferrisaurus and Gremlin to Leptoceratopsidae, but relationships within the group remain unresolved due to fragmentary fossils.
facts.quote: Further phylogenetic analysis added the new leptoceratopsid taxa Ferrisaurus and Gremlin, but the inclusion of these taxa and the fragmentary nature of many early ceratopsians resulted in a lack of resolution of leptoceratopsid relationships

facts.statement: It is debated whether Leptoceratops is unrelated to other forms, belongs within Protoceratopsidae, or forms a clade with genera like Montanoceratops and Udanoceratops.
facts.quote: where Leptoceratops was either unrelated to other forms, within Protoceratopsidae, or outside Protoceratopsidae but forming a clade with taxa like Montanoceratops, Udanoceratops, or Asiaceratops

facts.statement: When first described, the tail neural spines of Leptoceratops were the longest known for any ceratopsian.
facts.quote: when Leptoceratops was first described, they were the longest of any ceratopsian known at that time

facts.statement: Leptoceratops was traditionally assumed to be a quadruped.
facts.quote: Traditionally, Leptoceratops has been assumed to be quadrupedal.

facts.statement: Leptoceratops had forelimbs long enough to reach the ground upright, enabling a quadrupedal posture.
facts.quote: The forelimbs of Leptoceratops are long enough to reach the ground upright, allowing for quadrupedality.

facts.statement: Leptoceratops lacked opposable digits for one-handed grasping but could hold objects with two hands while moving bipedally.
facts.quote: Leptoceratops lacks opposable digits to allow for one-handed prehension, but would have been able to hold with two hands when moving bipedally.

facts.statement: Fossils from the Hell Creek Formation suggest that Leptoceratops was capable of scratch-digging or burrowing.
facts.quote: Scratch-digging is also believed to have been possible in Leptoceratops based on its forelimb anatomy, which is supported by fossils from the Hell Creek Formation suggesting burrowing.

facts.statement: In 2019, researchers proposed that Leptoceratops bonebeds represent adults buried during burrow collapses in multi-generational burrows.
facts.quote: Denver Fowler and colleagues presented in 2019 the belief that the sites instead represent adults buried during burrow collapses in a multi-generational burrow.

facts.statement: The fused cervical vertebrae (syncervical) in Leptoceratops likely evolved for digging rather than supporting a large head or combat.
facts.quote: The evolution of the syncervical in small-bodied neoceratopsians shows that it was likely not an adaptation for a large head or intraspecific combat.

facts.statement: Leptoceratops was a herbivore.
facts.quote: Leptoceratops, like other ceratopsians, would have been a herbivore.

facts.statement: Leptoceratops had a unique arcing bite path that created curved wear patterns on its teeth, differing from other neoceratopsians.
facts.quote: The unique wear pattern on teeth of Leptoceratops is inconsistent with the standard chewing of neoceratopsians, indicating that the bite included an arcing path to create the curved tooth wear seen.

facts.statement: Leptoceratops possessed a mammal-like orbital jaw motion during chewing, a trait unique among dinosaurs.
facts.quote: The mastication of Leptoceratops is different from all other dinosaurs, with the jaw undergoing an orbital motion that is mammal-like, despite the very large differences in jaw joint anatomy between Leptoceratops and analogous mammals.

facts.statement: Leptoceratops fossils from the Hell Creek Formation date from approximately 67.20 million years ago to the end of the Cretaceous.
facts.quote: The Hell Creek Formation in contrast lasts from earlier in the Maastrichtian, approximately 67.20 mya, to the end.

facts.statement: The formations containing Leptoceratops fossils consist largely of sandstone and mudstone attributed to floodplain environments.
facts.quote: These formations are composed largely of sandstone and mudstone, which have been attributed to floodplain environments.

facts.statement: It is debated whether Leptoceratops was as ecologically restricted to cool environments as previously thought, given its presence in coastal plain formations.
facts.quote: With the Triceratops/Edmontosaurus fauna being from coastal plains, Leptoceratops is not as ecologically restricted as previously thought.

facts.statement: By the time of the Hell Creek Formation, the landscape where Leptoceratops lived was dominated by angiosperms in a forest of small trees.
facts.quote: by the time of the Hell Creek angiosperms were dominant in a forested landscape of small trees.

facts.statement: Although traditionally linked to Protoceratopsidae, Leptoceratops is now placed in its own family, Leptoceratopsidae, alongside dinosaurs like Udanoceratops and Prenoceratops.

facts.statement: Remains have been found throughout western North America, including the Scollard Formation in Alberta, Canada, and the Lance Formation in Wyoming, USA.

facts.statement: Given its small size and quadrupedal posture, Leptoceratops would likely have been a low browser.
